name: Umiray Dumaget Agta
confidence_why: MacLeod's 1963 phoneme sketch says stress is not phonemic and falls on the final syllable, but Antonio's 2007 grammatical sketch from the same village (Matawe, Dingalan) treats accent as contrastive, with roots accented on the penult (qé:yen, bénli, sé:di) or the ultima (qidém, tantú) and shifts under affixation, and MacLeod's own long-vowel minimal pairs (laapis 'pencil' vs lapis 'tuna-like fish') together with the accented Umiray forms in Reid 1994 (órat, dumáwet vs tapúk) point the same way, so a contrastive penult-or-final accent is the better-supported reading even though the two first-hand descriptions disagree on the type of system.

new_statements.quote: Umirey Dumagat has two classes of phonemes. There are sixteen consonants: /b/, /k/, /d/, /g/, /h/, /l/, /m/, /n/, /ŋ/, /p/, /r/, /s/, /t/, /w/, /y/ and glottal stop /'/. There are six vowels: /a/, /ɔ/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/. Stress does not appear to be phonemic. It occurs on word final syllables. /ina/ (iná) 'mother' /ina na/ (ina na) 'mother mine' [fn. 2: Marked for stress. Also note that all examples in this paper are written phonetically (indicated by brackets) only when they differ from the phonemic writing.]
new_statements.citation: MacLeod, Thomas R. 1963. The phonemes of Umirey Dumagat and a suggested orthography. Unpublished ms., Summer Institute of Linguistics (Philippines). SIL Language & Culture Archives no. 74657, 16 pp.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 2 'Synopsis', typescript p. 2 (p. 3); footnote 2 on the Footnotes page (p. 16)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (16 pp., SIL archive 74657; text unusable, so I rendered the page scan and read them). p.3 (typescript p.2), sec. '2. SYNOPSIS' reads exactly: 'Umirey Dumagat has two classes of phonemes. There are sixteen consonants: /b/, /k/, /d/, /g/, /h/, /l/, /m/, /n/, /ŋ/, /p/, /r/, /s/, /t/, /w/, /y/ and glottal stop /'/.[fn 1] There are six vowels: /a/, /ɔ/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/. Stress does not appear to be phonemic. It occurs on word final syllables. /ina/ (iná)[fn 2] 'mother' /ina na/ (iná na) 'mother mine''. p.16 'FOOTNOTES' no. 2: 'Marked for stress. Also note that all examples in this paper are written phonetically (indicated by brackets) only when they differ from the phonemic writing.' --…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the final syllable of the word (illustrated with iná 'mother'; the enclitic phrase /ina na/ is given as a second hand-accented example).
new_statements.exceptions: None in MacLeod 1963 (hedged: 'does not appear to be phonemic'). Caveat from the later Antonio 2007 MA thesis: it treats accent and vowel length as distinctive vowel features and transcribes many roots with penultimate accent plus length ([tó:tul] 'walk', [bé:yed] 'pay', [mé:nit], [qéyen] 'no') beside final-accented roots ([regút], [gumatáŋ], [dumatóŋ]), and states that accent shifts to the ultima under -in/-an suffixation and retracts to the penult with maka-; so a Tagalog-type contrast may exist that MacLeod's preliminary analysis did not register.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('word final syllables') from isolated citation forms; the accent placement in the phrase example /ina na/ is hand-drawn and ambiguous in the scan. Preliminary phonemic statement based on 1961-62 fieldwork at Matawe, Dingalan, Quezon.
new_statements.identity_note: MacLeod 1963 describes the 'Umirey Dumagat dialect' as spoken at sitio Matawe, c. 8 km south of Dingalan, Quezon (Umiray River area = geographic centre; endonyms 'tagi keelogen'/'source Umirey' and 'tagibulus'), i.e. core Umiray Dumaget [umir1236], not the Anglat/Palaui Island varieties Glottolog lists as dialects. Antonio 2007 describes the same language under the name Tagebulos (Reid 1994: 'In Bulacan, the people refer to themselves as Tagabulos').

sources.citation: Antonio, Victor Corpus. 2007. Gramatikal na Iskets ng Tagebulos. MA thesis (Linggwistiks), Unibersidad ng Pilipinas-Diliman. 98 pp. (archive.org item antonio-gramatikal-na-iskets-ng-tagebulos_202402). In Filipino.
sources.note: Ch.2 (generative, SPE-style): 'aksent' (2.3.21) and 'lengt' (2.3.20) are listed among the distinctive features of vowels; no statement of where word accent falls. Sec. 2.5.2.3: with verb suffixes -in/-an 'May paglipat ng aksent sa ultima' (accent shifts to the ultima), e.g. /witik+-qan/ > [witikán]; 2.5.2.7 with maka- accent retracts to the penult ([maká:mit]). Transcriptions show both final ([regút], [gumatáŋ], [dumatóŋ]) and penult-with-length ([tó:tul], [bé:yed], [mé:nit], [qéyen]) accent on roots, i.e. data inconsistent with purely fixed final stress.

sources.note: 'This squib describes three theoretically challenging phonological processes found in the Manide, Inagta Alabat, and Umiray Dumaget languages spoken on the large northern Philippine island of Luzon.. A brief background survey of vocalic changes triggered by voiced stops is given, followed by the puzzling changes that depart from this more general pattern.' Segmental (voiced-stop-triggered vowel changes); no tone content expected; Umiray forms will carry Lobel's accent marks. Full text behind the MUSE paywall (page answered 'Verification required').
